summary: Given the diversity of experiments, file formats and levels of documentation, this project enables the integration of quantitative and qualitative information from physical experiments within the Physical Sciences Informatics system, facilitating the study and comparison of different combustion systems experiments in microgravity while reducing the complexity of data processing and interpretation. The Flame in Freefall program gathers, organizes, and analyzes NASA scientific data on an interactive platform. It allows users to view graphs, compare results, consult original documents, and export information, making data analysis easier by eliminating the need to open each file individually. The program was developed in Python, using Streamlit to create an interactive interface. It employs libraries such as Pandas for data processing, SQLite for storing information, Plotly for generating charts, and Pint for unit conversion. It is also capable of reading CSV, Excel, PDF, and ISA-Tab files.
details:
CONTEXT AND PHYSICAL DESCRIPTION OF PROBLEM

The study of combustion in microgravity is a field that lies at the intersection of fluid mechanics, thermodynamics, and chemical kinetics. In microgravity the mechanisms of mass transport and heat propagation can change, the absence of gravity alters the geometry of a flame and its dynamics, and under certain conditions it also affects how a fire might start, grow, spread, and, crucially, how it can be extinguished.

Gravity masks various physical and chemical phenomena that occur during these processes, microgravity by contrast allows for the isolation and simplification of the analysis of heat and mass transport, as well as reaction chemistry. The experiments conducted by NASA aim to further our understanding of the fundamental physics of combustion and to apply this knowledge toward fire safety and prevention in habitats and crewed spacecraft. The various experimental trials have yielded a range of qualitative and quantitative results. This enables scientists to isolate and directly study chemical kinetics and the transport of mass and heat—free from the interference of buoyancy-driven turbulence, which would otherwise complicate calculations—thereby validating numerical models that were previously impossible to test on Earth.

NASA has investigated these phenomena through experiments in reduced gravity and aboard the International Space Station, alongside computational and ground-based research. Their findings are relevant to spacecraft fire safety because an enclosed, ventilated cabin behaves differently from a conventional terrestrial environment. Material flammability, the movement of smoke particles, and the conditions required to extinguish a flame must be examined with these differences in mind.

Under normal gravity (1-g), the conservation equations for momentum, mass, and energy must account for a three-dimensional, unsteady buoyancy term; however, by eliminating gravity, mathematical models can be reduced to one-dimensional systems (such as spherical flames). This simplifies both the analytical and numerical solutions for the heat and mass transfer equations coupled with chemical reactions. Consequently, various parameters within the fields of reactive transport phenomena and heat and mass transfer are employed to define the stability limits and dynamics of a flame. This necessitates the integrated analysis of different types of data, while also addressing the challenge regarding the scope and extent of data collected in physicochemical experiments. A further difficulty is the volume and variety of scientific information produced by these investigations. Experimental conditions may be stored in CSV tables, numerical predictions in separate datasets, and interpretations in technical reports or presentations. Comparing such records requires attention to the origin of each value, its physical units, and whether it represents a measurement, a simulation, or a calculated quantity.

NASA PSI COMBUSTION SCIENCE DATA

The three NASA PSI experiments studied and applied to the program deal with reactive systems under microgravity conditions, yet they differ in terms of the physical state of the fuel and the geometry of the problem. PSI-117 considers isolated liquid hydrocarbon droplets; PSI-159 examines spherical diffusion flames fueled by gases; and PSI-62 focuses on flame propagation over solid materials. This distinction determines the specific features the program employs to extract and analyze data from these experimental sources.

The availability of documentation may vary depending on the experiment being analyzed. Regarding the data used for the application of the program, the PSI-117 dataset includes CSV files containing analyzed data along with a spreadsheet identifying the test conditions; the PSI-159 dataset includes metadata, a final report, and engineering documentation; and, finally, the PSI-62 dataset includes only descriptive metadata, with no corresponding reports or numerical tables.

The project uses publicly available combustion research data from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository, including twelve investigations: PSI-25, PSI-26, PSI-62, PSI-68, PSI-69, PSI-98, PSI-99, PSI-100, PSI-101, PSI-102, PSI-117, and PSI-159. Three additional studies received particular attention: PSI-62 (DOI: 10.60555/e9xp-ex83), PSI-117 (DOI: 10.60555/gz0q-b577), and PSI-159 (DOI: 10.60555/cyt1-kh64). Their materials were incorporated according to the types of evidence available, including investigation metadata, experimental reference data, numerical simulation results, engineering reports, and calculated parameters.

SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT AND DATA PROCESSING

Github:

https://github.com/kiriworks-co/flame-in-freefall

To work with the different NASA datasets, we developed Flame in Freefall as an interactive web application using Python and Streamlit. The objective was to provide a way to examine scientific records without requiring users to download, open, and interpret every source file independently.

The data-processing system reads CSV spreadsheets, XLSX workbooks, PDF documents, and ISA-Tab metadata. It extracts numerical tables and documentary passages while retaining the original files, and the structured information is stored in SQLite databases, which are also used to organize investigations, tables, document references, and scientific observations. Applying a classification scheme based on numerical values ​​makes it possible to distinguish between experimental conditions, reported results, simulation outputs, calculated quantities, and metadata. This is particularly relevant for some experiment as PSI-117, where experimental references and computational results may appear side by side. The program also handles physical units conservatively, utilizing the Pint library whenever the source information allows for a conversion. Missing units are not automatically inferred.

The interface uses Plotly for interactive graphs, data exploration, statistical summaries, and result exports. It also supports PDF visualization and dataset compatibility checks based on variables and units. Document retrieval combines SQLite FTS5 with semantic embeddings, providing access to 15,524 searchable scientific passages represented by 384-dimensional vectors. A lexical search alternative is available when the semantic model is not installed.

The system promotes evidence-based responses through source-linked passages and automated checks of citations, numerical values, and scientific categories. Google Gemini can optionally generate short explanations, but all core features remain available without external language-model APIs.

We also provides two guided exploration paths. One introduces combustion behavior in microgravity through physical explanations and NASA examples. The other examines prevention, smoke detection, and flame suppression in spacecraft. More detailed tools remain available through the investigation catalog, Data Explorer, comparison interface, and Scientific Assistant.

ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE

OpenAI Codex and Google Antigravity was used as AI-assisted development tools while building the web application. They helped with Python programming, debugging, interface development, automated testing, and technical documentation.

The application also includes local semantic search and an optional Google Gemini integration for evidence-based explanations. Its core data exploration and retrieval features work without Gemini. The Gemini integration was implemented and tested with simulated API responses, but a live API connection had not been validated in the documented development stage.
